newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - BEER AND OSTRICHES - BY TONY TWINE.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - BEER AND OSTRICHES - BY TONY TWINE.

text.p: By Tony Twine, an economist at Econometrix financial consultancy
What, I hear you ask, can the connection be between beer and ostriches?

Until the weekend just past, I doubt very much whether there was one, but a sequence of personal experiences on Saturday brought one possible connection into what I laughingly refer to as my conscious mind.

Having been delighted to hear the news of South African Breweries' (SAB) successful issue in the foreign capital market, which had been 80 percent oversubscribed, she who must be obeyed (to borrow Mr. Mortimor's phrase) and I set off to a branch of a major chain store in one of the leafiest of Johannesburg's northern suburbs.
Let us just say that it had one of those hyped-up store names, and leave it at that.
One of several objectives which we had in mind was to purchase some ostrich meat which, we are all told by the health fundies, is good for us because of its low fat and cholesterol content.
One could almost feel the arterial tissue and heart muscle relaxing as we strode into the store.

It is probably just as well that the wife and I eat fairly healthily. The next 90 minutes turned out to be the stuff that coronary disease is made of, cardiovascular stress simply does not come into it.

I must not bore you with the details of the initial cause of the hypertension. Briefly, an objective to purchase a cordless telephone and an answering machine, which should have taken no more than 10 or 15 minutes, ended up taking more than an hour.

Assisted, if that is the right word, by someone whose bearing, rather than his competence, suggested that he was a supervisor, we eventually came to understand that at least half the stock displayed on the shelves was not or sale -- quite what it was doing on display continues to baffle us.

During the prolonged exercise, our man went to answer two telephone calls, and became involved in the fruitless task of remonstrating with his own staff and the woman in charge of the compact disc department about the company policy towards a customer who wanted to buy a cheap CD with a 100 rand voucher.

Eventually, we reached the point of paying for our purchases of telecommunications hardware. For the entire period so far elapsed, a young male assistant had stood steadfastly by his till, studiously ignoring the telephone which the supervisor had to keep excusing himself to answer.

The young man's efforts were, would you believe, largely a waste of time, because nothing short of dynamite would open the till -- certainly not the computerised operating system which was clearly no more efficient than its human operators.
The Donald Duck staff and the Mickey Mouse point of sale equipment were doing much better than the Disney cartoons running in the TV section next door.

So, with blood pressure raised 25 percent above desirable levels, we proceeded to the butchery section. An enquiry to a shelf packer as to where we could find ostrich meat produced a typical "over there", together with a raised arm, cocked at an indefinite angle which could have indicated anything in range from one metre to the equator.

Homing-in, a second and similar enquiry made to a man in a butcher's apron, produced a more definite stabbing of the finger, together with another brusque "over there". Closer inspection revealed that he had pointed to stewing steak, which comes with far too many legs to be confused with ostrich meat.

When eventually located, the flesh of the large fowl was poorly packed, with blood oozing from the packaging -- where, one wondered for a horrified moment, had the bird been terminated? Behind that screen over there?

A request for additional clingfilm brought a steady stare from a gaggle of female employees, each of whom was doing an impression of Lot's wife. Fortunately, a butcher of alternate ethnic origin came to the rescue, possibly galvanised by the fact that the bleeding package was now being waved in the general direction of the kosher meat section.

These are only the bare bones of our shopping experience which can best be described as a total cock-up. Sorry, Mr. Ostrich, the phrase is not intended to apply to you -- you were the only thing in the shop to display any sense of commitment.
But where lies the link between ostriches and beer? The nature of SAB's capital coup provides the answer.
The 1.5 billion rand raise by Breweries is for the expansion of their overseas interests. Who could really blame them for wanting to expand their interests there, rather than back home.

Whether you are brewing beer or retailing communications hardware or food, the South African economy certainly seems to have far too many jobs, and far too few workers -- people who really work, that is, not those who are simply employed.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
